2017A16.goal: Horse $k$ is at the start exactly at multiples of $k$ minutes. We want the first time $T>0$ when at least $5$ horses are at the start together. That is the smallest number with at least $5$ divisors among $1,\ldots,10$.

tools.name: Common return time
tools.fact: \text{Horses }k_1,\ldots,k_m\text{ meet at the start at multiples of }\operatorname{lcm}(k_1,\ldots,k_m)
tools.why: Each horse is there exactly at multiples of its lap time.

tools.name: Divisors in a range
tools.why: Horse $k$ is at the start at time $T$ iff $k\mid T$.

2017A16.approach: Rephrase: find the smallest $T$ with at least $5$ divisors from $\{1,\ldots,10\}$. Check small $T$ by counting such divisors; $T$ needs many small divisors, so try highly composite numbers.

steps.title: Rephrase with divisors
steps.explain: Horse $k$ is at the start at time $T$ exactly when $k\mid T$. So we need the least $T$ with at least $5$ divisors among $1$–$10$.

check.q: At time $T=8$, which horses are at the start?
How many divisors does $12$ have that are at most $10$?
What is the digit sum of $12$?

2017A16.bridge: Find the least $T$ with five divisors among $1$ to $10$.
solution: Horse $k$ is at the start at time $T$ iff $k\mid T$.
Numbers below $12$ have at most $4$ divisors in $\{1,\ldots,10\}$.
2017A16.shortcut: Ignore the given $S=2520$; it is the lcm of all ten and not needed.
2017A16.recognize: "When are these periodic things together again" means lcm; "at least $m$ of them" means a number with many small divisors.

2017A17.goal: The lattice points on $x^2+y^2=25$ are $(\pm5,0),(0,\pm5),(\pm3,\pm4),(\pm4,\pm3)$. Among irrational chord lengths, we want the largest divided by the smallest.

tools.name: Chord length formula
tools.why: For points on a circle of radius $5$: $|P-Q|^2=|P|^2+|Q|^2-2P\cdot Q$.

tools.name: Irrational distances
tools.fact: \sqrt{m}\text{ is irrational iff }m\text{ is not a perfect square}
tools.why: Distances between lattice points are square roots of integers.

2017A17.approach: Find the largest non-square value of $|PQ|^2$ and the smallest. Since $|PQ|^2=50-2P\cdot Q$, make the dot product as negative as possible without being $-25$ (the diameter, length $10$, rational), and find the closest pair.

steps.title: Largest irrational distance
steps.explain: $(3,4)$ and $(-4,-3)$ have dot product $-24$, so $|PQ|^2=98$ and $PQ=7\sqrt2$. Only diameters do better, and they have length $10$.

check.q: What is the squared distance from $(3,4)$ to $(-4,-3)$?

steps.title: Smallest irrational distance
steps.explain: The closest points are neighbours like $(3,4)$ and $(4,3)$: $|RS|^2=2$, $RS=\sqrt2$.

check.q: What is the distance from $(4,3)$ to $(5,0)$?

steps.title: Ratio
steps.explain: $\tfrac{7\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}=7$.

2017A17.bridge: List the $12$ lattice points, find the longest and shortest irrational chords.
2017A17.shortcut: Points $(a,b)$ and $(-b,-a)$ are nearly opposite: distance $\sqrt2(a+b)=7\sqrt2$ for $a+b=7$.
2017A17.recognize: Lattice points on a circle: list them from sums of two squares; chord lengths come from the dot product formula.

2017A18.goal: Amelia (heads with probability $\tfrac13$) and Blaine ($\tfrac25$) alternate, Amelia first; the first head wins. We want Amelia's winning probability. The game "resets" after each full round with no heads.

tools.name: Restart equation
tools.why: Amelia wins now, or both miss and the situation repeats.

tools.name: Geometric series
tools.why: Equivalent to summing Amelia's chances over rounds.

2017A18.approach: Condition on the first round: either Amelia wins immediately, or both miss and we are back where we started. Solve the resulting linear equation for $P$.

steps.title: One round
steps.explain: Amelia wins on her first toss with probability $\tfrac13$. Both miss with probability $\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac35=\tfrac25$, and then the game restarts.

check.q: What is the probability both miss in one round?

steps.title: Solve
steps.explain: $P=\tfrac13+\tfrac25P$, so $\tfrac35P=\tfrac13$ and $P=\tfrac59$. Then $q-p=9-5=4$.

2017A18.bridge: Write the restart equation and solve for $P$.
traps: Forgetting the factor for Blaine missing.
2017A18.recognize: Alternating "first success wins" games: one round plus a restart gives a linear equation.

2017A19.goal: Five people sit in a row; Alice cannot be next to Bob or Carla, and Derek cannot be next to Eric. Alice's restrictions are the strongest, so casework on Alice's seat is natural.

tools.name: Casework on the most constrained person
tools.fact: \text{Alice's neighbours must be Derek or Eric}
tools.why: Bob and Carla are forbidden next to her.

tools.name: Multiplication principle
tools.why: Once Alice and her neighbours are placed, the rest is independent.

2017A19.approach: Place Alice first. Her neighbours can only be Derek and Eric. If she is at an end she has one neighbour; in the middle positions she has two, which must be exactly Derek and Eric (who are then not adjacent to each other). Count each case.

steps.title: Alice at an end
steps.explain: Say seat $1$. Seat $2$ is Derek or Eric ($2$ ways). Say Derek; then Eric cannot be in seat $3$, so Eric is in seat $4$ or $5$ ($2$ ways), and Bob, Carla fill the rest ($2$ ways): $2\cdot2\cdot2=8$. Same for seat $5$: $16$ total.

check.q: Alice in seat $1$, Derek in seat $2$. How many seats can Eric take?

steps.title: Alice not at an end
steps.explain: Alice in seat $2$, $3$ or $4$ has two neighbours, which must be Derek and Eric ($2$ orders); they sit on opposite sides of Alice, so they are not adjacent. Bob and Carla fill the other two seats ($2$ ways): $4$ for each of $3$ positions, $12$.

check.q: Alice in seat $3$: how many arrangements?
check.why: $2$ orders of Derek/Eric beside her, $2$ for Bob/Carla.

2017A19.bridge: Case on Alice's seat; her neighbours must be Derek and Eric.
solution: Alice's neighbours must come from Derek and Eric.
Alice at an end: $2\cdot2\cdot2=8$ per end, $16$ total.
Alice in a middle seat: Derek and Eric on either side ($2$), Bob and Carla in the rest ($2$): $4$ each, $12$ total.
2017A19.shortcut: Complementary counting is messier here; casework on the most restricted person is cleanest.
traps: Forgetting Derek and Eric cannot be adjacent when Alice is at an end.
2017A19.recognize: Row seating with "not next to" rules: place the most restricted person first and case on their position.

2017A20.goal: $S(n)=1274$ and we must decide which value $S(n+1)$ could take. Adding $1$ changes digits only at the end: trailing $9$s become $0$s.

tools.name: Digit sum after adding 1
tools.why: If $n$ ends in $k$ nines, those become zeros ($-9k$) and the next digit goes up by $1$.

tools.name: Digit sum mod 9
tools.why: $10\equiv1\pmod9$.

2017A20.approach: Either use the formula $S(n+1)=1275-9k$, or note $S(n+1)\equiv S(n)+1\equiv1275\equiv6\pmod9$. Check which choice is $6\pmod9$.

check.q: If $n$ ends in three $9$s, how does $S(n+1)$ compare with $S(n)$?

steps.title: Test the choices mod 9
steps.explain: $S(n+1)\equiv1275\equiv1+2+7+5=15\equiv6\pmod9$. Choices: $1\equiv1$, $3\equiv3$, $12\equiv3$, $1239\equiv6$, $1265\equiv5$. Only $1239$ works ($k=4$).

solution: Adding $1$ to a number ending in $k$ nines gives $S(n+1)=S(n)+1-9k=1275-9k$.
2017A20.shortcut: Digit sums mod $9$ equal the numbers mod $9$, so $S(n+1)\equiv n+1$.
2017A20.recognize: Digit sums before and after adding $1$: trailing nines and the mod-$9$ invariant.

2017A21.goal: Two squares sit in a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle: one at the right-angle corner (side $x$), one with a side on the hypotenuse (side $y$). We want $\tfrac xy$. Similar triangles give each side.

tools.name: Square at the right angle
tools.why: The square's far corner lies on the hypotenuse $\tfrac{X}{a}+\tfrac{Y}{b}=1$ with $X=Y=x$.

tools.name: Square on the hypotenuse
tools.why: The triangle above the square is similar to the whole, with height $h-y$ and base $y$: $\tfrac{y}{c}=\tfrac{h-y}{h}$.

tools.name: Altitude to the hypotenuse
tools.why: Area two ways.

2017A21.approach: For $x$, put the corner at the origin: the square's far vertex $(x,x)$ lies on the hypotenuse. For $y$, use the altitude: the small triangle above the square is similar to the whole triangle with ratio $\tfrac{h-y}{h}$, and its base is $y$.

steps.title: Find $x$
steps.explain: Hypotenuse $\tfrac X4+\tfrac Y3=1$ through $(x,x)$: $\tfrac x4+\tfrac x3=1$, so $x=\tfrac{12}7$.

steps.title: Find $y$
steps.explain: The altitude is $h=\tfrac{12}5$. The triangle above the square is similar to the whole with height $h-y$ and base $y$: $\tfrac{y}{5}=\tfrac{h-y}{h}$, so $y=\tfrac{5h}{5+h}=\tfrac{12}{37/5}=\tfrac{60}{37}$.

steps.title: Ratio
steps.explain: $\tfrac xy=\tfrac{12/7}{60/37}=\tfrac{12\cdot37}{7\cdot60}=\tfrac{37}{35}$.

2017A21.bridge: Use the hypotenuse line for $x$ and similar triangles with the altitude for $y$.
2017A21.shortcut: Remember both formulas: corner square $\tfrac{ab}{a+b}$, hypotenuse square $\tfrac{ch}{c+h}$.
traps: Assuming both squares are the same size.
2017A21.recognize: Squares inscribed in triangles: use similar triangles (or the line equation) with one side of the square along a side of the triangle.

2017A22.goal: A circle is tangent to sides $AB$ and $AC$ of equilateral triangle $ABC$ at $B$ and $C$. We want the fraction of the triangle outside the circle. The part inside is a circular segment cut off by chord $BC$.

tools.name: Tangent ⟂ radius
tools.why: Radius to the point of tangency.

tools.name: Central angle
tools.why: Quadrilateral $ABOC$ has two right angles.

tools.name: Segment area
tools.why: Remove the triangle $OBC$ from the sector.

2017A22.approach: The circle's centre $O$ is beyond $BC$ (away from $A$). Inside the triangle, the circle covers only the segment between chord $BC$ and the $120^\circ$ arc. Compute $r$ from the tangents, the segment area, and the fraction.

steps.title: Radius
steps.explain: Let the side be $s$. Triangle $ABO$ has a right angle at $B$ and $\angle BAO=30^\circ$, so $r=OB=s\tan30^\circ=\tfrac{s}{\sqrt3}$.

steps.title: Segment inside the triangle
steps.explain: $\angle BOC=120^\circ$. The segment area is $\tfrac13\pi r^2-\tfrac{\sqrt3}4r^2=r^2\left(\tfrac\pi3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}4\right)=s^2\left(\tfrac\pi9-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{12}\right)$.

steps.title: Fraction outside
steps.explain: The triangle has area $\tfrac{\sqrt3}4s^2$. Outside fraction $=1-\dfrac{\pi/9-\sqrt3/12}{\sqrt3/4}=1-\tfrac{4\pi}{9\sqrt3}+\tfrac13=\tfrac43-\tfrac{4\sqrt3\pi}{27}$.

2017A22.bridge: Find $r$ from the tangents, compute the $120^\circ$ segment, and take $1-$ its share of the triangle.
solution: The circle meets the triangle in the segment of area $r^2(\tfrac\pi3-\tfrac{\sqrt3}4)=s^2(\tfrac\pi9-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{12})$.
traps: Taking the circle as the incircle.
Using the major segment instead of the minor one.
2017A22.recognize: Circles tangent to two sides at their endpoints: the centre lies on the angle bisector, and the central angle is $180^\circ$ minus the vertex angle.

2017A23.goal: We count triangles with vertices among the $25$ points of a $5\times5$ grid. Choose any $3$ points and subtract the collinear triples.

tools.name: Complementary counting
tools.why: Three points form a triangle unless collinear.

tools.name: Lines in a $5	imes5$ grid
tools.why: Three collinear grid points need a step $(d_x,d_y)$ fitting twice in a span of $4$.

2017A23.approach: $\binom{25}3=2300$. Count collinear triples by direction: rows, columns, the two diagonal directions, and the steep/shallow slopes $\pm2,\pm\tfrac12$. Larger steps cannot fit three points.

steps.title: Rows, columns, diagonals
steps.explain: Each row has $\binom53=10$ triples: $50$ for rows, $50$ for columns. Diagonals of slope $1$ have lengths $5,4,4,3,3$: $10+4+4+1+1=20$; same for slope $-1$: $40$ total.

check.q: How many triples on a line of $4$ points?

steps.title: Slopes $pm2$ and $pm	frac12$
steps.explain: Slope $2$ needs points $(i,j),(i+1,j+2),(i+2,j+4)$: $j=1$ and $i=1,2,3$, so $3$ triples. Each of the four slopes $\pm2,\pm\tfrac12$ gives $3$: $12$.

check.q: Can three grid points with step $(1,3)$ fit in a $5\times5$ grid?

2017A23.bridge: Total triples minus collinear triples, counted by direction.
solution: Collinear: rows $50$, columns $50$, diagonals $40$, slopes $\pm2,\pm\tfrac12$: $12$; total $152$.
2017A23.shortcut: Remember the diagonal count $2(10+4+4+1+1)=40$ for a $5\times5$ grid.
2017A23.recognize: Triangles from grid points: total minus collinear triples, organised by the step vector between consecutive points.

2017A24.goal: Every root of the cubic $g$ is a root of the quartic $f$, so $g$ divides $f$: $f(x)=g(x)(x-k)$. Matching coefficients finds $k$, $a$, $b$, $c$, and then $f(1)=g(1)(1-k)$.

tools.name: Factor from shared roots
tools.fact: g\text{ has distinct roots, all roots of monic }f\ \Rightarrow\ f=g\cdot(x-k)
tools.why: $f$ has degree $4$ and contains the three linear factors of $g$.

tools.name: Matching coefficients
tools.why: Expand and compare with $f$.

2017A24.approach: Write $f=g\cdot(x-k)$. The $x$-coefficient gives $10-k=100$ immediately, so $k=-90$. Then the $x^3$ coefficient gives $a$. Finally evaluate $f(1)=g(1)(1-k)$ without needing $b$ or $c$.

steps.title: Set up the factorisation
steps.explain: $f(x)=(x^3+ax^2+x+10)(x-k)$. Comparing $x$-coefficients: $10-k=100$, so $k=-90$.

steps.title: Find $a$
steps.explain: $x^3$-coefficient: $a-k=1$, so $a=1+k=-89$.

2017A24.bridge: Write $f=g(x-k)$, match two coefficients, and evaluate at $1$.
solution: $f(x)=g(x)(x-k)$ since $g$'s three distinct roots are roots of $f$.
2017A24.recognize: "Every root of $g$ is a root of $f$" means $g\mid f$; write the quotient with unknown coefficients and match.

2017A25.goal: We count $3$-digit numbers that can be rearranged into a $3$-digit multiple of $11$. Work from the multiples of $11$: group them by digit multiset, and count all $3$-digit arrangements of each multiset.

tools.name: Divisibility by 11
tools.why: Alternating digit sum; for $3$ digits it is between $-8$ and $18$.

tools.name: Arrangements of a multiset
tools.fact: 3\text{ distinct digits}: 6;\ \text{one repeat}: 3;\ \text{minus those with leading }0
tools.why: Standard permutation counts.

tools.name: Avoid double counting
tools.fact: \overline{abc}\text{ and }\overline{cba}\text{ are both multiples, same multiset}
tools.why: $a-b+c$ is symmetric in $a$ and $c$.

2017A25.approach: List multiples of $11$ by type: those with a $0$, those with $b=a+c$, and those with $b=a+c-11$. Each type gives a family of digit multisets. For each multiset, count its $3$-digit arrangements, and add (the multisets are all different).

steps.title: Multiples containing $0$
steps.explain: $c=0$: $a=b$, giving $110,220,\ldots,990$: multisets $\{a,a,0\}$, each with $2$ valid arrangements ($aa0,a0a$): $18$. $b=0$: $a+c=11$: multisets $\{2,9,0\},\{3,8,0\},\{4,7,0\},\{5,6,0\}$, each with $4$ arrangements: $16$.

check.q: How many $3$-digit arrangements of the digits $3,8,0$?

steps.title: Nonzero, $b=a+c$
steps.explain: $a=c$: $121,242,363,484$: multisets $\{a,a,2a\}$ with $3$ arrangements each: $12$. $a\ne c$ with $a+c\le9$: $16$ multisets of three distinct digits, $6$ arrangements each: $96$.

check.q: How many unordered pairs $\{a,c\}$ of distinct positive digits have $a+c\le9$?

2017A25.bridge: Group multiples of $11$ by digit multiset and count each multiset's $3$-digit arrangements.
solution: $b=a+c$: $4$ multisets with a repeat ($12$) and $16$ with distinct digits ($96$).
2017A25.shortcut: There are $81$ multiples of $11$; most come in pairs $abc,cba$ sharing a multiset with $6$ arrangements.
traps: Forgetting arrangements with a leading zero are not $3$-digit.
2017A25.recognize: "Some permutation has property $P$": count the multisets that have it, then all arrangements of each, avoiding double counting.
